newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU grain export caution may hit market share - ONIC.
newsitem.headline: EU grain export caution may hit market share - ONIC.

text.p: Drought stricken North-Africa should be a major wheat buyer this year but French exporters are already losing sales to the region because the European Commission is maintaining a cautious stance on exports, officials from France's grain office ONIC said on Wednesday.

ONIC's president Michel Marie told a news conference that a European Union decision to convene its grain panel only every two weeks in July and August was "a handicap" for exporters as it hurt the image of the EU as a reliable grain supplier.
The EU panel that adjudicates grain exports traditionally meets each week.
"We regret that the committee will meet only every two weeks...In the meantime we lose markets, " said Michel Marie.
"What this means is that nothing gets done between July and August. There are (export) opportunities but we do not seize them," he added.

Director general Alain Moulinier said dry conditions were expected sharply to cut grain production in North Africa, driving the region, a traditional outlet for French wheat, to step up imports in the 1997/98 season.
"For us in terms of export prospects that's heavy," he said.
North African grain buyers recently returned to the world market to take advantage of a sharp decline in prices caused by active harvesting in the United States.
But the region has bought mostly wheat from the United States since April when the EU halted grain exports to keep a lid on domestic prices ahead of new harvest.

Last week the EU agreed to open its new round of export tenders for the 1997/98 season. Weekly bidding for export subsidies for wheat, barley and rye is due to re-open on July 17 when the EU grain panel meets again.
But EU grain officials have said they were in no hurry to export as they want to get a clearer picture of the new harvest.
Moulinier said he did not expect the EU would take any action at the July 17 meeting.
"This will be an observation round, nothing else," he said.

Besides North Africa, Egypt and Iraq should be of major interest for French trade next year. But competition is looming from eastern European nations like Romania and Hungary that expect a much better harvest and will seek to export excess supplies at the start of the new season, he said.

In the 1996/97 campaign France exported 6.25 million tonnes of soft wheat to non-EU destinations. This included 3.2 million tonnes destined to countries that either used to be or were never traditional outlets for French wheat, including Egypt, Iraq, Poland, Turkey, and Indonesia.
Moulinier said this meant that for the new 1997/98 season France would need to grab business opportunities as they came because there was no such thing as a secure outlet for French wheat.
